content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued a recommendation regarding the screening of pregnant women for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) to prevent early-onset Group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease in newborns. This recommendation is based on evidence from observational studies, primarily conducted in high-income countries, which suggest that either universal or risk-based screening strategies may reduce the risk of early-onset GBS disease compared to no screening strategy. GBS infection, caused by Streptococcus agalactiae, affects over 390,000 newborns annually and is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis. Early-onset GBS (EOGBS) disease is defined by the presence of GBS in the newborn’s blood, cerebrospinal fluid, or other sterile sites within the first seven days after birth. EOGBS infection can be prevented by administering IAP to pregnant women before delivery. The risk of EOGBS infection can be determined through two primary methods: (1) identifying maternal GBS colonization in the vagina, perineum, or rectum, or (2) assessing maternal risk factors associated with EOGBS disease. The WHO outlines several approaches to determine eligibility for IAP: 1. Universal Screening: All pregnant women undergo antepartum culture-based screening using rectovaginal swabs. IAP is administered to those with evidence of GBS colonization. 2. Risk Factor-Based Screening: IAP is administered to pregnant women with one or more risk factors for EOGBS, without swabbing for maternal GBS colonization. 3. Combined Strategy: A combination of universal screening and risk-based screening programs. 4. No Specific Screening Strategy: IAP is administered based on individual clinical assessment. Risk factors typically considered in the risk-based approach include maternal fever, rupture of membranes, bacteriuria, and a history of a previous child with EOGBS. However, these factors may vary across different settings. Regardless of the strategy, most pregnant women with known GBS bacteriuria (e.g., detected through urine testing for urinary tract infection) or a previous child affected by EOGBS will receive IAP. The WHO recommends offering either universal antenatal testing for GBS colonization with IAP for women who test positive or intrapartum assessment of risk factors with IAP for women at risk of having a newborn with EOGBS disease. This recommendation is intended for health professionals responsible for developing national and local healthcare guidelines and protocols, as well as those providing care to women and their newborns during labor and childbirth. This includes midwives, nurses, general medical practitioners, obstetricians, maternal and child health program managers, and relevant staff in ministries of health and training institutions. The guideline development process followed WHO’s standard operating procedures, including identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination and implementation. The evidence supporting the recommendation was synthesized using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. A systematic review was conducted to prepare evidence profiles for the prioritized questions. The WHO convened a meeting of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) on December 5–6, 2023, where members reviewed and deliberated on the strength and direction of the recommendation. The GDG considered the balance between desirable and undesirable effects, the certainty of evidence, values and preferences of women and families, resource requirements, cost-effectiveness, health equity, acceptability to stakeholders, and feasibility of implementation. The recommendation emphasizes the importance of screening pregnant women for IAP to prevent EOGBS disease in newborns. It encourages healthcare providers to refer to the accompanying remarks, evidence summaries, and considerations on implementation and research gaps to ensure the recommendation is correctly understood and applied in practice.
